edges.effect_quant: Across contemporary clinic-based studies, restless legs syndrome was present in 23.9% to 40.3% of adults with iron deficiency anemia, far above background prevalence estimates.
edges.mechanism: Iron deficiency can impair central dopaminergic signaling and reduce brain iron availability in regions involved in sensory discomfort and limb-movement control, which makes RLS biologically plausible in people with iron-deficient states.
edges.summary: Observational studies consistently report that restless legs syndrome is common among adults with iron deficiency anemia, with prevalence estimates often in the one-quarter to two-fifths range. The signal is clinically meaningful but still comes mainly from cross-sectional or clinic-based cohorts rather than large population meta-analyses, so the edge stays conservative.
edges.caveats: Most evidence is observational and enriched for symptomatic or referred patients, so the exact prevalence may not generalize to every community setting. These studies support screening and plausibility more than a precise causal effect size.
